prose.hook: Brazil shares common boundaries with every South American country except Chile and Ecuador — nine neighbours, plus the French territory of French Guiana. It is the largest country in South America and in the Southern Hemisphere, mostly flat to rolling lowland behind a narrow coastal belt, and most of the Pantanal, the world's largest tropical wetland, extends through its west. What it sends the world follows from that scale: soybeans, crude petroleum, iron ore, raw sugar and corn, drawn from a mineral list that also runs to bauxite, gold, manganese, tin, niobium, rare earth elements and uranium.
prose.physicalGeography: Mostly flat to rolling lowlands in the north, with plains, hills and mountains elsewhere and a narrow coastal belt along the Atlantic. That combination of low relief and enormous extent is what makes agriculture at continental scale possible.
prose.climate: Mostly tropical, turning temperate in the south — a range wide enough that the same country sees recurring drought in the northeast and occasional frost in the south. Flooding is a regular hazard in the southern states.
prose.economy: The largest economy in Latin America and upper-middle-income, driven substantially by domestic consumption rather than exports alone. Brazil is a member of Mercosur, BRICS and the G20 and a candidate for OECD accession. Its industrial base is unusually broad for a major commodity exporter — aircraft, motor vehicles and parts, steel, chemicals, cement, textiles and footwear. Inequality in income and in access to health and education remains high.
prose.peopleAndCulture: Portuguese is the official language, which makes Brazil the only Portuguese-speaking country in a continent that otherwise speaks Spanish. By self-identification the population is roughly 45% mixed, 44% White, 10% Black, with smaller Indigenous and Asian populations. Religiously it is majority Roman Catholic at around 57%, with Evangelical Christianity at about 27% and Afro-Brazilian traditions including Umbanda and Candomblé also present.
